top_choice_rationale: Michon is first on voice and formal achievement. From public knowledge and translation, his compressed French sentence is hard to attribute to anyone else. It is joined to a recurring inquiry into vocation, anonymity and the afterlife of obscure lives, and the later books appear to apply the method to new matter rather than repeat Small Lives and The Eleven. The case is narrower than Cărtărescu's in corpus size, so I cite consistency as evidence of sustained quality, not as proof of significance, and I would keep the citation to the unity of compression and subject. I have not independently verified any text. I could not confirm the later books, and translation loss is a risk for every candidate. Cărtărescu is second because his long forms plausibly extend rather than restate an earlier world, but that rests on structural description, not on a comparison of passages. Wright is third because her formal departure from oral practice is serious, but I cannot judge whether her achievement is repeated or concentrated in two novels. Adonis is fourth because I cannot assess Arabic prosody without specialist reading of the originals, and that is a limit on my access, not a verdict on the poetry. No award is last, since each proposal names a writer with a serious claim on the criteria.
